summary: This Wikipedia-derived note covers several episodes in Universal Pictures' history: the late-1960s and 1970s productions of producer Hal B. Wallis, the 1950s deal by agent Lew Wasserman that gave James Stewart a share of profits instead of a salary, the company's 1912 incorporation and vertically integrated studio structure, and its losing rights to Oswald the Lucky Rabbit after Walt Disney's Mickey Mouse rose to prominence. The passages move between film financing, Academy Award nominations, and animation history.
one_line: Overview of Universal Pictures' history, covering its 1912 founding, Hal Wallis's late productions, the Wasserman-Stewart profit deal, and the Oswald rabbit animation rights.
key_facts: Hal B. Wallis moved from Paramount to Universal, where he produced Anne of the Thousand Days (1969) and Mary, Queen of Scots (1971).
Anne of the Thousand Days was nominated for Best Picture, Best Actor (Richard Burton), Best Actress (Geneviève Bujold), and Best Supporting Actor (Anthony Quayle).
Wallis retired from Universal after making Rooster Cogburn (1975), a sequel to True Grit (1969) that he had produced at Paramount.
Rooster Cogburn co-starred John Wayne, reprising his Oscar-winning role, and Katharine Hepburn, their only film together.
Rooster Cogburn was only a moderate success.
In 1950 MCA agent Lew Wasserman made a deal with Universal for his client James Stewart.
Wasserman's deal gave James Stewart a share in the profits of three pictures in lieu of a large salary.
Winchester '73 proved to be a hit, and the profit-share arrangement became the rule for many future Universal productions.
The Universal Film Manufacturing Company was incorporated in New York on April 30, 1912.
Carl Laemmle emerged as president of Universal in July 1912 and was the primary figure in the partnership.
Universal was a vertically integrated company, with production, distribution and exhibition linked in one corporate entity.
Universal owned the rights to the Oswald the Lucky Rabbit character, which Walt Disney and Ub Iwerks had created.
Charles Mintz unsuccessfully demanded that Disney accept a lower fee for producing the Oswald property.
Disney and Iwerks created Mickey Mouse, who starred in Steamboat Willie in 1928, the first "sync" sound animated short.
Universal subsequently severed its link to Mintz and formed an in-house animation studio headed by Walter Lantz to produce Oswald cartoons.
